Nissaya-vagga Kimatthiya-sutta (The Discourse on the Purpose)
(AN 11.1, PTS AN v 311) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“For what purpose, Bhante, are wholesome virtues, and what is their benefit?
“Wholesome virtues, Ānanda, have non-remorse as their purpose and non-remorse as their benefit.”
“But, Bhante, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of freedom from remorse?
“Freedom from remorse, Ānanda, has gladness as its purpose and gladness as its benefit.
“But, Bhante, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of gladness?”
“Joy, Ānanda, has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of rapture?
“Rapture, Ānanda, has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit.”
“But, Bhante, for what purpose is tranquility, and what is its benefit?
“Tranquility, Ānanda, has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit.
“But, Bhante, for what purpose is happiness, and what is its benefit?”
“Happiness, Ānanda, has concentration as its purpose and concentration as its benefit.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of concentration?
“Concentration, Ānanda, has the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its purpose and the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its benefit.”
“But, venerable sir, for what purpose and with what benefit is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are?
“Knowledge and vision of things as they really are, Ānanda, has disenchantment as its purpose and disenchantment as its benefit.
“But, venerable sir, for what purpose and with what benefit is disenchantment?”
“Disenchantment, Ānanda, has dispassion as its purpose and dispassion as its benefit.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of dispassion?
“Dispassion, Ānanda, has the knowledge and vision of liberation as its purpose and the knowledge and vision of liberation as its benefit.”
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-regret as their purpose and non-regret as their benefit;
non-regret has gladness as its purpose and gladness as its benefit;
gladness has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit.
Rapture has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit; tranquility has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit;
happiness has concentration as its purpose and concentration as its benefit.
Concentration has the purpose and benefit of knowing and seeing things as they really are;
knowing and seeing things as they really are has the purpose and benefit of disenchantment;
disenchantment has the purpose and benefit of dispassion.
Dispassion has the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation; its benefit is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtues lead step by step to the supreme goal. Thus ends the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.2 1.

Nissaya-vagga Cetanākaraṇīya-sutta The Discourse on What is to be Done through Volition “Monks, there are these eleven things that are to be done through volition by one who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness. What eleven? (1) One should dwell with a mind free from ill will. (2) One should dwell with a mind free from harshness. (3) One should dwell with a mind free from envy. (4) One should dwell with a mind free from miserliness. (5) One should dwell with a mind free from deceit. (6) One should dwell with a mind free from guile. (7) One should dwell with a mind free from obstinacy. (8) One should dwell with a mind free from vehemence. (9) One should dwell with a mind free from pride. (10) One should dwell with a mind free from arrogance. (11) One should dwell with a mind free from conceit. These, monks, are the eleven things that are to be done through volition by one who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness.”
“Bhikkhus, for one who is virtuous, endowed with virtue, there is no need for an intentional resolve:
‘May non-regret arise in me.’”
It is the natural law, monks, that non-regret arises in one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue.
For one who has no regret, monks, there is no need for an act of will, thinking:
"May joy arise in me."
It is the natural law, monks, that joy arises in one who is without remorse.
For one who is joyful, monks, there is no need for an intentional effort:
"May rapture arise in me."
It is the natural law, monks, that rapture arises in one who is gladdened.
For one whose mind is filled with rapture, monks, no volitional effort need be made to think:
"May my body become tranquil."
It is the natural law, monks, that for one whose mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil.
For one whose body is tranquil, monks, there is no need for volition to think:
"I am experiencing pleasure."
This is the natural law, monks: one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness.
For one who is happy, monks, no volitional effort need be made to think:
"May my mind become concentrated."
It is the natural law, monks, that the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
For one who is concentrated, monks, there is no need for volition, thinking:
"May I know and see things as they truly are."
It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is concentrated knows and sees according to reality.
For one who knows and sees according to reality, monks, there is no need for a volitional act to think:
"I am becoming disenchanted."
This is the natural law, monks: one who knows and sees things as they truly are becomes disenchanted.
For one who is disenchanted, monks, no volitional effort need be made to think, "May I become dispassionate."
It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is disenchanted becomes dispassionate.
For one who is dispassionate, monks, there is no need for an act of will:
"May I realize the knowledge and vision of liberation."
This is the natural law, monks: that one who is dispassionate realizes the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, monks, dispassion has the knowledge and vision of liberation as its purpose and the knowledge and vision of liberation as its benefit;

disenchantment has dispassion as its purpose and dispassion as its benefit; knowledge and vision of things as they really are has disenchantment as its purpose and disenchantment as its benefit; concentration—

Knowledge and vision according to reality has knowledge and vision according to reality as its purpose and knowledge and vision according to reality as its benefit; concentration has happiness as its purpose and concentration as its benefit;

tranquility has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit; rapture has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit; joy has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit;
non-remorse has joy as its purpose and joy as its benefit; and wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose.
“...having non-remorse as their benefit.
Thus, monks, phenomena flow into phenomena, phenomena fulfill phenomena, for the purpose of going from the near shore to the far shore. This is the second [discourse].

Nissaya-vagga First Discourse on the Proximate Cause (Paṭhama-upanisā-sutta)
“Bhikkhus, for one who is immoral,
for one deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no non-regret, for one deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for gladness is destroyed.”
When there is no gladness, for one devoid of gladness, joy has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no joy, for one devoid of joy, tranquility has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no tranquility, for one devoid of tranquility, happiness has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no happiness, for one deprived of happiness, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no right concentration, for one deprived of right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, for one deprived of knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no disenchantment, for one devoid of disenchantment, the proximate cause for dispassion is destroyed.
When there is no dispassion, for one devoid of dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is deprived of its proximate cause.
Just as, monks, when a tree is deprived of its branches and foliage, its bark does not reach full development, nor its inner bark, nor its softwood, nor its heartwood reaches full development.
In the same way, monks, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, non-regret lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no non-regret, for one who is deficient in non-regret, joy lacks its proximate cause... [and so on] ...
up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Monks, for one who is virtuous, endowed with virtue, non-regret is a supporting condition.
When there is non-regret, for one endowed with non-regret, joy is a supporting condition.
When there is joy, for one endowed with joy, rapture is a supporting condition.”
When there is rapture, for one possessed of rapture, the necessary condition for tranquility is fulfilled;
when there is tranquility, for one possessed of tranquility, the necessary condition for happiness is fulfilled;
when there is happiness, for one possessed of happiness, the necessary condition for right concentration is fulfilled.
When right concentration exists, for one endowed with right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is possessed of its proximate cause.
When the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are exists, for one endowed with the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment is possessed of its proximate cause.
When disenchantment exists, for one endowed with disenchantment, dispassion is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is dispassion, for one endowed with dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its proximate cause.
Just as, monks, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its shoots reach full development, its bark... its softwood... and its heartwood also reach full development;
even so, monks, for one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue, non-regret possesses its proximate cause.
"When there is freedom from remorse, for one endowed with freedom from remorse, the proximate cause is fulfilled...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
This is the third.

Nissayavagga Dutiyaupanisāsutta (The Second Discourse on the Underlying Causes)
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus."
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, for one who is immoral, for one deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who has failed in freedom from remorse, joy lacks its proximate cause;
when there is no joy, for one who has failed in joy, rapture lacks its proximate cause;
when there is no rapture, for one who has failed in rapture, tranquility lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no tranquility, for one deficient in tranquility, the necessary condition for happiness is destroyed;
when there is no happiness, for one deficient in happiness, the necessary condition for right concentration is destroyed;
when there is no right concentration, for one deficient in right concentration, the necessary condition for the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is destroyed.
When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one deficient in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment is destroyed;
when there is no disenchantment, for one deficient in disenchantment, the proximate cause for dispassion is destroyed;
when there is no dispassion, for one deficient in dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
"Friend, just as when a tree is deprived of its branches and foliage, its bark does not reach full development, nor its inner bark, nor its softwood, nor its heartwood reaches full development;
even so, friend, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no non-regret, for one who is deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for gladness is destroyed... [and so on]."
the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For one who is virtuous, friend, who is endowed with virtue, non-regret is supported by that condition;
when there is non-regret, for one who is endowed with non-regret, joy is supported by that condition.
When there is gladness, for one possessed of gladness, joy is present as its supporting condition;
when there is joy, for one possessed of joy, tranquility is present as its supporting condition;
when there is tranquility, for one possessed of tranquility, happiness is present as its supporting condition.
When there is happiness, for one possessed of happiness, right concentration possesses its proximate cause;
when there is right concentration, for one possessed of right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are possesses its proximate cause;
when there is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one possessed of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment possesses its proximate cause.
When there is disenchantment, for one endowed with disenchantment, the necessary condition for dispassion is fulfilled.
When there is dispassion, for one endowed with dispassion, the necessary condition for the knowledge and vision of liberation is fulfilled.

Just as, friends, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its bark reaches full development, its inner bark reaches full development, its softwood reaches full development, and its heartwood also reaches full development.
"In the same way, friends, for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue, non-regret is a proximate cause.
When there is non-regret, for one accomplished in non-regret, joy is a proximate cause... [and so on] ...

The Third Discourse on the Underlying Condition (Tatiyaupanisāsutta).
There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “… [as before] …”
“Friends, for one who is immoral, for one deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no non-regret, for one deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for gladness is destroyed.
When there is no gladness, for one deficient in gladness, the proximate cause for rapture is destroyed.”
When there is no rapture, for one devoid of rapture, the proximate cause for tranquility is destroyed;
when there is no tranquility, for one devoid of tranquility, the proximate cause for happiness is destroyed;
when there is no happiness, for one devoid of happiness, the proximate cause for right concentration is destroyed.
When right concentration is absent, for one deficient in right concentration, the prerequisite for knowing and seeing things as they truly are is destroyed.
When knowing and seeing things as they truly are is absent, for one deficient in knowing and seeing things as they truly are, the prerequisite for disenchantment is destroyed.
When disenchantment is absent, for one deficient in disenchantment, the prerequisite for dispassion is destroyed.
When dispassion is absent, for one who has failed in dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.
Just as, friend, a tree that has failed in its branches and foliage does not reach fullness in its shoots, nor in its bark, nor in its softwood, nor in its heartwood;
even so, friend, for one who is immoral and has failed in virtue, non-regret lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who has failed in freedom from remorse, joy lacks its proximate cause...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For one who is virtuous, friend, for one perfected in virtue, freedom from remorse possesses its proximate cause.
When there is freedom from remorse, for one endowed with freedom from remorse, joy is possessed of its proximate cause;
when there is joy, for one endowed with joy, rapture is possessed of its proximate cause;
when there is rapture, for one endowed with rapture, tranquility is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is tranquility, for one possessed of tranquility, happiness is possessed of its proximate cause;
when there is happiness, for one possessed of happiness, right concentration is possessed of its proximate cause;
when there is right concentration, for one possessed of right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one endowed with knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is disenchantment, for one endowed with disenchantment, dispassion is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is dispassion, for one endowed with dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is possessed of its proximate cause.

"Friend, just as a tree endowed with branches and foliage has its outer bark reach full development, its inner bark reach full development, its softwood reach full development, and its heartwood reach full development;
even so, friend, for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue, non-regret is supported by that foundation.
When there is non-regret, for one who possesses non-regret, joy is supported by that foundation... [and so on]..."

The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.6
1. The Chapter on Dependence:
Discourse on Calamities (Byasanasutta) (AN 11.6, PTS AN v 317)

“Bhikkhus, for that bhikkhu who is abusive, reviling, and a slanderer of noble ones toward his fellow celibates, it is possible and within the range of occurrence that he will meet with one or another of eleven calamities.
What are these eleven?
He does not attain what has not yet been attained.”
One falls away from what has been attained;
one does not purify oneself in the true Dhamma;
or one becomes conceited regarding the true Dhammas.
Either he leads the holy life without being satisfied with it,
or he commits some defiled offense,
or he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
Or he is afflicted by a severe illness or affliction,
or he falls into madness or mental derangement,
or he dies deluded.

With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell—that monk, bhikkhus, who is abusive, reviling, and a slanderer of noble ones toward his fellow celibates; it is possible, it is within the bounds of possibility, that he will meet with one or another of these eleven calamities.

That monk, bhikkhus, who is abusive, reviling, and a slanderer of noble ones toward his fellow celibates; it is impossible, it is not within the bounds of possibility, that he will not meet with one or another of these eleven calamities.
Of which eleven?
He does not attain what has not been attained;
he falls away from what has been attained.
They do not purify themselves in the true Dhamma,
or they are conceited regarding the true Dhamma,
or they lead the holy life without delighting in it.
Or he commits some defiled offense,
or having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life,
or he is afflicted by a severe illness.
One either falls into madness or mental derangement,
dies deluded,
and with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
“Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a monk who is abusive, reviling, and a slanderer of his fellow celibates would not meet with one or another of these eleven calamities.

1. The Chapter on Dependence: The Discourse on Perceptions (Saññāsutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these three perceptions. What three? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, and the perception of the repulsiveness of food. These, bhikkhus, are the three perceptions. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-established in these three perceptions, he is capable of abandoning the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasures, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he is capable of uprooting the underlying tendency to conceit, of destroying the underlying tendency to craving for existence, and of attaining final Nibbāna in this very life. “Bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of death. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, when one perceives death, one does not give rise to lust for sensual pleasures, nor does one give rise to aversion, nor does one give rise to views; one does not give rise to conceit, nor does one give rise to craving for existence. Therefore, bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of death. “Bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of non-self. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, when one perceives non-self, one does not give rise to lust for sensual pleasures, nor does one give rise to aversion, nor does one give rise to views; one does not give rise to conceit, nor does one give rise to craving for existence. Therefore, bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of non-self. “Bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of the repulsiveness of food. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, when one perceives the repulsiveness of food, one does not give rise to lust for sensual pleasures, nor does one give rise to aversion, nor does one give rise to views; one does not give rise to conceit, nor does one give rise to craving for existence. Therefore, bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of the repulsiveness of food. “Bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of impermanence. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, when one perceives impermanence, one does not give rise to lust for sensual pleasures, nor does one give rise to aversion, nor does one give rise to views;

one does not give rise to conceit, nor does one give rise to craving for existence. Therefore, bhikkhus, if one were to say of anything that it is the foremost of all perceptions, it is this: the perception of impermanence. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-established in these five perceptions, he is capable of abandoning the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasures, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he is capable of uprooting the underlying tendency to conceit, of destroying the underlying tendency to craving for existence, and of attaining final Nibbāna in this very life. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking thus, he did so thinking: ‘These three perceptions are beneficial; they lead to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. But if I were to teach them to the bhikkhus now, their minds would not be inclined toward listening, and they would not gain confidence in me. “Friends, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

"Could it be, Bhante, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth in earth, nor perceive water in water, nor perceive fire in fire, nor perceive air in air..."

He would perceive air, but he would not perceive the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space; he would not perceive the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness;
he would not perceive the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness; he would not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he would not perceive this world as this world, nor the other world as the other world.
“Furthermore, Ānanda, would he not be percipient even regarding that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and ranged over by the mind,
yet he would still be percipient? “It is possible, Ānanda,
that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he is no longer percipient of earth as earth...”
He would not perceive water in water; he would not perceive fire in fire; he would not perceive air in air;
he would not perceive the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space; he would not perceive the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness;
he would not perceive the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness; he would not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He would not perceive this world as "this world," nor would he perceive the other world as "the other world"; even regarding that which is seen,
heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and investigated by the mind, he would have no perception therein—
and yet, he would still be percipient."
“But how, venerable sir, might a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth, nor water as water,
nor fire as fire, nor air as air, nor the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness?”

He would have the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, but not the perception of the base of nothingness; he would have the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, but not the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he would have the perception of this world, but not the perception of the other world; he would have the perception of the other world, but not the perception of this world;
nor would he have the perception of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or investigated by the mind.
“Even there, he would not be percipient, yet he would still be percipient.
“In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is percipient thus:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’”
"In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu may attain such a state of concentration that he does not perceive earth as earth,
nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air;
he does not perceive the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness."

He would have the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, but not the perception of the base of nothingness; he would have the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, but not the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he would have the perception of this world, but not the perception of the other world; he would have the perception of the other world, but not the perception of this world;
and as for whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or examined by the mind—[he would have no perception thereof].
"Even there, he would not have perception, yet he would still possess perception.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, the Venerable...
He exchanged greetings with Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, could it be that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would no longer [perceive] the earth?"
“He might be percipient of earth … [and so on] … he might not even be percipient of that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and circumspected by the mind;
yet he would still be percipient.
“It is possible, friend Ānanda, for a bhikkhu to attain such a state of concentration that he is neither percipient of earth in earth,” and so forth.
“He would not perceive that... [and so on] ...even regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered by the mind, he would not perceive it there;
yet he would still be one who perceives.
“But in what way, friend Sāriputta, could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration?”

“Would he not perceive earth as earth … [and so on] … nor would he perceive anything that is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or examined by the mind; yet he would still be percipient?
“In this case, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu is percipient in this way:”
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
It is in this way, friend Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth...
[and so on] ...nor even with regard to what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, and examined by the mind.
“...by mind; even there, he would not be percipient, yet he would still be percipient.
“It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend!
That the meaning and the phrasing of both the Teacher and his disciple coincide and harmonize, and do not conflict, regarding this very supreme state!”
"Just now, friend, having approached the Blessed One, I asked him about this matter.
The Blessed One also explained this matter to me using these very same words, phrases, and syllables, just as the Venerable Sāriputta has done.
It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend!"
"For indeed, where the meaning of both the Teacher and the disciple coincides in meaning and the phrasing coincides in phrasing, and they do not dispute one another— namely,
regarding the supreme state. (The Seventh) Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.8
1. The Chapter on Reliance:
The Discourse on Attention (Manasikārasutta) (AN 11.8, AN 11.9, PTS AN v 321)

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Could it be, Bhante, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not attend to the eye, nor attend to forms, nor attend to the ear, nor attend to sounds?”
One should not attend to the nose, nor attend to odors; one should not attend to the tongue, nor attend to tastes;
one should not attend to the body, nor attend to tangibles;
one should not attend to earth, nor attend to water, nor attend to fire, nor attend to air.
One should not attend to the base of infinite space; one should not attend to the base of infinite consciousness;
one should not attend to the base of nothingness; one should not attend to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one should not attend to this world; one should not attend to the other world; nor to whatever is seen or heard here.
“Should one not attend to what is sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and investigated by the mind,
yet still attend [to something]?
“It is possible, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not attend to the eye.”
One should not attend to form; one should not attend to the ear; one should not attend to sound;
one should not attend to the nose; one should not attend to odor; one should not attend to the tongue;
one should not attend to taste; one should not attend to the body; one should not attend to tangibles; one should not attend to earth.
One should not attend to water; one should not attend to fire; one should not attend to air;
one should not attend to the base of infinite space; one should not attend to the base of infinite consciousness; one should not attend to the base of nothingness;
one should not attend to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; one should not attend to this world.
"One should not attend to the world beyond, nor should one attend to whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after,
or pondered by the intellect; yet one should indeed attend [to this]."
“But how, venerable sir, might a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not attend to the eye,
nor attend to forms … [and so on] … nor even attend to that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, and examined by the mind,
yet he would still be attending?”
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu attends to this:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not attend to the eye, nor would he attend to forms … [and so on] …”
One should not attend to whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or investigated by the mind;
yet one should attend [to this] as well.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.9 1. Nissaya-vagga Saddha-sutta “Monks, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, and is firmly established for full enlightenment. What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, monks, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, and is firmly established for full enlightenment.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.

Then the Venerable Saddha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Saddha was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Saddha, meditate with the meditation of a thoroughbred horse;
do not meditate with the meditation of a wild colt.
And how, Saddha, is there the meditation of a wild colt?
For the wild colt, Saddha, tied to the feeding trough, broods over the fodder, thinking, "Fodder, fodder!
Why is that? Because it does not occur to the wild colt tied to the trough: [that he might go elsewhere].
“What task will the horse-tamer have for me today? How shall I perform it?
Thus, while tied to the feeding trough, he meditates only on “grass, grass.
In the same way, Saddha, here a certain wild colt of a man, whether gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, [behaves in this manner].
He dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overcome by sensual lust, and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
Making that very sensual lust his internal basis, he meditates, he meditates intensely, he meditates thoroughly, he meditates repeatedly.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will...
he dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor...
he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse...
He dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt and overwhelmed by doubt; he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen doubt.
Taking doubt itself as his internal support, he meditates, meditates deeply, meditates intensely, and meditates thoroughly.
He meditates supported by earth, he meditates supported by water, he meditates supported by fire, and he meditates supported by air.
One meditates depending on this; one meditates depending on the base of infinite space; one meditates depending on the base of infinite consciousness;
one meditates depending on the base of nothingness; one meditates depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one meditates depending on this world; one meditates depending on the other world; and one meditates depending on what is seen and heard here.
Whatever has been sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind—relying on that as well, he meditates.
In this way, Saddha, there is the meditation of a wild colt among men.
And how, Saddha, is there the meditation of a thoroughbred?
For a noble thoroughbred horse, Saddha, tied to his feeding trough, does not brood, thinking, "Fodder, fodder! Why is that?
Because, Saddha, it occurs to that noble thoroughbred horse tied to the trough: [as follows].
“What task will the horse-tamer have for me today? How shall I respond to him?
Thus, though bound to his manger, he does not dwell on the thought, “Fodder! Fodder!
For, Saddha, that noble thoroughbred horse regards the taking up of the goad as a debt, as a bond, as a loss, and as a calamity.
In the same way, Saddha, a noble thoroughbred of a person, whether gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut,
does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, nor is he overcome by sensual lust;
and he understands, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will;
he does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor;
he does not dwell with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by doubt, nor one overcome by doubt; he understands, as it truly is, the escape from arisen doubt.
He does not meditate depending on earth, nor does he meditate depending on water, nor fire, nor air;
he does not meditate depending on the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness.
He meditates without depending on the base of nothingness; he meditates without depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he meditates without depending on this world; he meditates without depending on the other world;
and he does not meditate depending on whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect.
And he meditates.
And as he thus meditates, Saddha, the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, and together with Pajāpati, pay homage from afar to that noble thoroughbred of a man:
"Homage to you, O thoroughbred of a man!"
"Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not understand that upon which you rely as you meditate."
When this was said, the Venerable Saddha addressed the Blessed One:
"But how, Bhante, does a noble thoroughbred person meditate, not depending on earth to meditate,
not depending on water to meditate, not depending on fire to meditate, not depending on air to meditate, and not depending on the base of infinite space?"
He meditates without depending on the base of infinite space; he does not meditate depending on the base of infinite consciousness; he does not meditate depending on the base of nothingness;
he does not meditate depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he does not meditate depending on this world; he does not meditate depending on the other world;
nor does he meditate depending on anything seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or mentally pondered.
"Even that which has been examined by the mind, he does not meditate by depending on that.
Yet he does meditate.
And how, venerable sir, does that noble thoroughbred person meditate, such that the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, and together with Pajāpati, pay homage to him from afar?"
"Homage to you, O noble steed among men!
Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not fully comprehend that [power] of yours."
“And what is it, Saddha, depending on which you meditate?
“Here, Saddha, for a well-bred thoroughbred man, the perception of earth regarding earth has been eliminated;
the perception of water regarding water has been eliminated; the perception of fire regarding fire has been eliminated; the perception of air regarding air has been eliminated.”

In the base of infinite space, the perception of the base of infinite space has become manifest; in the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has become manifest;

in the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of nothingness has become manifest; in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has become manifest;
in this world, the perception of this world has become manifest; in the other world...

The perception of the world has become resolved; even regarding that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered by the mind, there too perception has become resolved.
It is for one meditating thus, Saddha, that a noble steed of a person does not meditate in dependence on earth... [and so forth]...
Even that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered by the mind— one does not meditate depending on that,
yet one does meditate. And when he meditates in this way,
Saddha, the gods together with Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati pay homage from afar to that noble thoroughbred of a person.
"Homage to you, O noble steed among men!
Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not fully comprehend that which belongs to you."
“That too is what you rely upon when you meditate.
(The Ninth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.10
1. The Chapter on Dependence:
The Discourse on the Peacock’s Feeding Ground (AN 11.10, AN 11.11, PTS AN v 326)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a bhikkhu has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation; he is the best among gods and humans.”
Which three?
The aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, and the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training.

Possessing these three qualities, monks, a bhikkhu has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation; he is the best among gods and humans.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a bhikkhu is one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation; he is the best among gods and humans.
What are the three?
The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.”

“Monks, a monk endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation—the best among gods and humans.

Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with another three qualities is one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation—the best among gods and humans.
Which three?”

“Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation— the best among gods and humans. Monks,

a bhikkhu endowed with two qualities is one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation— the best among gods and humans.”
Which two?
Clear vision and conduct.

Endowed with these two qualities, monks, a bhikkhu has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation; he is the best among gods and humans.
“Bhikkhus, this verse was spoken by Brahmā Sanankumāra:
‘Among those who rely on lineage, the khattiya is the best in this world;’”
"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct, he is the best among gods and humans.
Now, monks, this verse spoken by Sanankumāra was well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is beneficial, not unbeneficial; it is approved by me.
I too, monks, say this:
“The kshatriya is the best among those people who rely on lineage.”
“Endowed with true knowledge and conduct,
he is the best among gods and humans. Tenth.

Its summary verse:

And the proximate cause through calamity;
two perceptions, attention,

Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.11 2. Anussativagga Paṭhamamahānāmasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Mahānāma, when a noble disciple possesses four things, it is fitting for him to claim: ‘I am one who has arrived at the fruit, one who has reached the goal, one for whom the task is done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own purpose, one who has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one who is liberated through final knowledge. “What four? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

“He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, it is fitting for him to claim: ‘I am one who has arrived at the fruit... one who is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When a noble disciple possesses these four things, it is fitting for him to claim: “I am one who has arrived at the fruit... one who is liberated through final knowledge. “Venerable sir, I possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha. I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. But, venerable sir, I still have doubt about the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. “Mahānāma, since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, it is fitting for you to claim: ‘I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, it is fitting for you to claim: “I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. “Venerable sir, I possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha. I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. And I also have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. But, venerable sir, I still have doubt about the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints. “Mahānāma, since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, it is fitting for you to claim: ‘I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, it is fitting for you to claim: “I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. “Venerable sir, I possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha. I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. I have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. And I also have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints. But, venerable sir, I still have doubt about the attainment of Nibbāna here and now. “Mahānāma, since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, and since you have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints, it is fitting for you to claim: ‘I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, and since you have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints, it is fitting for you to claim: “I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. “Venerable sir, I possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha. I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. I have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. I have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints. And I also have some degree of faith in the attainment of Nibbāna here and now. But, venerable sir, I still have doubt about the final knowledge of arahantship. “Mahānāma, since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, and since you have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints, and since you have some degree of faith in the attainment of Nibbāna here and now, it is fitting for you to claim:

‘I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Since you possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha, and since you possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, and since you have some degree of faith in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, and since you have some degree of faith in the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints, and since you have some degree of faith in the attainment of Nibbāna here and now, it is fitting for you to claim: “I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. “
(AN 11.11, AN 11.12, PTS AN v 328) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Now on that occasion a number of bhikkhus were engaged in making a robe for the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One, having finished his robe-making, will set out on tour at the end of the three months.
Now Mahānāma the Sakyan heard it said:
“It seems many bhikkhus are making robes for the Blessed One.”
“‘When his robe is finished and the three months have passed, the Blessed One will set out on tour.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
‘I have heard this, Bhante:’”
“It seems, Bhante, that many bhikkhus are making robes for the Blessed One, thinking:
‘When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.
Since we are dwelling in various dwellings, by what kind of dwelling should we dwell?”
“Excellent, excellent, Mahānāma!
This is indeed worthy of you, sons of good family, that you have approached the Tathāgata and asked:
‘Venerable sir, among us who dwell in various dwellings, by which dwelling should we dwell?’”
“Mahānāma, one who has faith is successful, not one who lacks faith;
one who has aroused energy is successful, not one who is lazy;
one whose mindfulness is established is successful, not one who is muddled in mindfulness.”
One who is concentrated succeeds, not one who is unconcentrated;
one who possesses wisdom succeeds, not one who lacks wisdom.
Having established yourself, Mahānāma, in these five qualities, you should further develop six qualities.
In this regard, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Tathāgata thus:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind becomes straightened with reference to the Tathāgata.
Now, Mahānāma, a noble disciple whose mind is straightened gains the knowledge of the meaning, gains the knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

For one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.

“Mahānāma, this is called a noble disciple who dwells in balance amidst a generation that has fallen into imbalance; who dwells without malice amidst a generation full of malice; who, having entered the stream of the Dhamma, develops the recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Dhamma thus:
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be realized by the wise for themselves.’”
“Mahānāma, on whatever occasion a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;

He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... [as above] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
This too, Subhūti, is a manifestation of faith for one endowed with faith.
Furthermore, Subhūti, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, a bhikkhu [beholds beings...]
He sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views."
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.

But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body... [they have reappeared in a good destination].
‘After passing away, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
he sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bhikkhu, with the purified divine eye... [as before] ...understands beings according to their karma, this too, Subhūti, is a manifestation of faith for one endowed with faith.

Moreover, Subhūti, through the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.

“Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself and attained [the state of an arahant]—this too, Subhūti, is a ground for the faith of one endowed with faith.
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, those grounds for the faith of one endowed with faith that have been spoken of by the Blessed One exist in this bhikkhu; and this bhikkhu is seen to correspond to them.”

"Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is learned, one who has retained what he has heard and accumulated what he has heard;
those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which are entirely complete and pure—"
They praise the holy life; such teachings as these have been heard much by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated through right view.
This, venerable sir, is how a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
“Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is easy to correct … [as above] … he follows instruction.

Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is skillful and diligent regarding those various services for his fellow celibates; he possesses the ingenuity to find the appropriate means to perform them and to organize them effectively.
Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is a lover of the Dhamma, delights in what is well-spoken, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.”
"Venerable sir, this bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without toil, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

Venerable sir, this bhikkhu recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... [and so on]... thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes."
“Venerable sir, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, this bhikkhu … [as before] … understands beings according to their kamma.
Venerable sir, through the destruction of the taints, this bhikkhu … [as before] … enters and dwells in the realization of liberation.
Venerable sir, those qualities spoken of by the Blessed One as the manifestations of faith for one endowed with faith exist in this bhikkhu, and this bhikkhu is seen to be consistent with them.”
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
Therefore, Subhūti, you should dwell together with this bhikkhu Saddha.
And whenever you, Subhūti, wish to see the Tathāgata, you should approach the Tathāgata to see him together with this bhikkhu Saddha.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.15 2. Anussativagga (The Chapter on Recollections)
The Discourse on Loving-kindness (Mettāsutta): “Monks,

when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, eleven benefits are to be expected.”
What are the eleven? One sleeps happily; one awakens happily; one does not see evil dreams; one is dear to human beings;
one is dear to non-human beings; deities protect one; fire, poison, or weapons do not affect one; [one is mindful and clear-headed, and one’s faculties remain balanced].
“His mind quickly becomes concentrated; his facial complexion becomes serene; he dies unconfused;
and if he does not penetrate further, he is reborn in the Brahma-world.

Monks, when the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness is practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken, these eleven benefits are to be expected.”
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.16. 2.
Anussativagga (The Chapter on Recollections)
The Discourse to the People of Aṭṭhakanāgara (AN 11.16–17).
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.
Now at that time, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery where a certain bhikkhu was staying; having approached, he said this to that bhikkhu:
"Venerable sir, where is the Venerable Ānanda staying at present?"
“Venerable sir, we are indeed desirous of seeing the Venerable Ānanda.
“Householder, that Venerable Ānanda is staying at Vesālī, in the village of Beluva.
Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having completed his business in Pāṭaliputta, went toward Vesālī.

The householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Is there, venerable Ānanda, anything that has been taught by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—"
“Which one thing, when rightly proclaimed, leads a bhikkhu who dwells heedful, ardent,
and resolute to the liberation of an unliberated mind, to the destruction of the taints that have not yet been destroyed,
or to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained?”
“There is, householder, one thing well-expounded by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
wherein for a monk dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute,
the mind not yet liberated becomes liberated, or the taints not yet exhausted come to exhaustion, or that which has not been attained— ”
“He attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
“But, venerable Ānanda, what is that one thing which has been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant,
the perfectly enlightened Buddha— wherein a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute [attains this]?”
“Does an unliberated mind become liberated, or do the unabandoned taints go to their destruction,
or does one attain the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained?

“In this case, householder, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.”
Thus he reflects:
“This first jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced.
He understands: “Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.”
Established therein, one attains the destruction of the taints.

If one does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, through the total exhaustion of the five lower fetters, one becomes of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is a single Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It has been rightly proclaimed, wherein for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent,
ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the unabated taints reach their exhaustion,
or the unsurpassed security from bondage, not yet attained, is fully realized.

Furthermore, householder, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
... [and so on] ... the third jhāna;
... [and so on] ... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus he reflects:
"This fourth jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced.
He understands: "Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation."
Standing upon that, one attains the destruction of the taints.

If one does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the total exhaustion of the five lower fetters, one becomes spontaneously reborn (opapātiko), attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
This too, householder, is a single Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It has been rightly proclaimed, wherein for a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the mind that was not yet liberated becomes liberated, the taints that were not yet exhausted reach exhaustion,
and the unsurpassed security from bondage that had not yet been attained is reached.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, and measureless.
He dwells having pervaded [the world] with a measureless, enmity-free, and harm-free mind.
He reflects thus:
"This liberation of mind through loving-kindness is also conditioned and volitionally produced."
‘Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation,’ he understands.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is one who, by that Blessed One who knows... [as before] ...attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu with a mind imbued with compassion...
[as before] ...with a mind imbued with gladness... [as before].
He dwells having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere and in every way, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He reflects thus:
‘This liberation of mind through equanimity is also conditioned and volitionally produced.
He understands: ‘Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is a person who, by the Blessed One who knows... [as before] ...either attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been reached.

Furthermore, householder, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
He reflects thus:
‘This attainment of the base of infinite space is also conditioned and volitionally produced.’
‘Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation,’ he understands.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is one who, by that Blessed One who knows... [and so on] ...attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness...
[and so on] ...having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Thus he reflects:
"This attainment of the base of nothingness, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced.
He understands: "Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation."
Standing there, one attains the destruction of the taints.

If one does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is a person who, by the Blessed One who knows... [as before] ...attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been reached.”
When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Just as if, venerable Ānanda, a man seeking one entrance to a treasure were suddenly to find eleven entrances to treasures;
even so, venerable sir, while seeking one door to the Deathless, I have found eleven doors to the Deathless for my practice.”
“Venerable sir, it is just as if a man had a house with eleven doors. When that house was on fire, he would be able to make himself safe by way of even a single one of those doors.
In the same way, venerable sir, I shall be able to make myself safe by way of even a single one of these eleven doors to the Deathless.
For indeed, venerable sir, these followers of other sects will seek the teacher’s fee from their own teacher.”
"How could I not pay honor to the Venerable Ānanda?
Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from Vesālī and Pāṭaliputta, personally satisfied and served them with excellent hard and soft food.
He presented each bhikkhu individually with a pair of robes, and he presented the Venerable Ānanda with the triple robe.
He had five hundred dwellings built for the Venerable Ānanda.
This is the sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.17
