“Monks, a cowherd endowed with eleven factors is incapable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper.
With which eleven?
Here, monks, a cowherd does not know form, he is not skilled in characteristics, and he does not remove flies’ eggs...”
He does not heal wounds; he does not smoke [the incense]; he does not know the fords; he does not know when they have drunk;
he does not know the paths; he is not skilled in pastures; he milks the cows without leaving anything remaining;
and he does not show special honor to those bulls who are the fathers of the herd and the leaders of the herd.
“Monks, a cowherd endowed with these eleven factors is incapable of tending a herd of cattle or making it prosper.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eleven qualities is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the eleven? [The list follows].”
In this case, monks, a monk does not know form; he is not skilled in characteristics; he is not one who removes flies; he is not one who covers wounds;
he is not one who smokes; he does not know the ford; he does not know when [the water] has been drunk;
he does not know the path; he is not skilled in pastures; he milks dry; and as for those monks...
He does not honor with excessive veneration those elders who have known the Dhamma for a long time, who have been long gone forth, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha.
And how, monks, is a bhikkhu not one who knows form?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu does not understand as it really is any kind of form whatsoever—“the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.”
In this way, monks, a monk is not one who knows form.
And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in characteristics?
Here, monks, a monk does not understand as it really is: “The fool is characterized by his actions; the wise person is characterized by his actions.”
In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled in characteristics.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not remove flies?

Here, monks, a monk tolerates a thought of sensual desire that has arisen; he does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease. He tolerates a thought of ill will that has arisen… a thought of cruelty that has arisen… [in the same manner].
Whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he tolerates them; he does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not bring them to an end, and does not cause them to cease.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who does not remove flies.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not dress a wound?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk grasps at its general appearance and grasps at its secondary details.

Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the faculty of the eye.
One does not attain restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.
If, while dwelling with this faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—were to flow in after him, he does not practice for its restraint;
he does not guard the faculty of mind, nor does he achieve restraint over the faculty of mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who does not dress a wound.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not produce smoke?
Here, monks, a monk does not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has mastered it.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who does not produce smoke.
And how, monks, does a monk not know the ford?

Here, monks, a monk does not, from time to time, approach those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā, and he does not inquire or question them, saying:
"Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?"

Those venerable ones do not reveal what has not been revealed to you, nor do they clarify what has not been made clear; nor do they dispel your doubt regarding various matters that give rise to uncertainty.
In this way, monks, a monk does not know the ford.
And how, monks, does a monk not know when he has drunk?

“Here, bhikkhus, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a bhikkhu does not gain knowledge of the meaning, does not gain knowledge of the Dhamma, and does not gain joy connected with the Dhamma.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu does not know what has been drunk.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu not know the path?”
“Here, monks, a monk does not understand the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is.
In this way, monks, a monk does not know the path.
And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in the pasture?
"Here, monks, a monk does not understand the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are.
In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled regarding his pasture.
And how, monks, is a monk one who milks dry?"
"Here, monks, faithful householders invite a monk, offering robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. In that regard, the monk does not know moderation in receiving.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who milks dry.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not honor with extra veneration those elder monks who have long been ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha?"

In this case, monks, a monk does not maintain bodily action imbued with loving-kindness—both openly and in private—toward those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have long been gone forth, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha;
nor does he maintain verbal action imbued with loving-kindness... nor does he maintain mental action imbued with loving-kindness—both openly and in private.

"In this way, monks, a monk does not honor with extra respect those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha.
Possessing these eleven qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Monks, a cowherd endowed with eleven factors is capable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper."
By which eleven? Here, monks,
a cowherd is knowledgeable about forms, skilled in characteristics, one who removes flies, one who dresses wounds,
one who prepares smoke, one who knows the watering place, one who knows when they have drunk, and one who knows the path.
He knows [the pastures]; he is skilled in his range; he milks [the cows] leaving a remainder; and he honors with special respect those bulls who are fathers and leaders of the herd.
It is by being endowed with these eleven qualities, monks, that a cowherd is capable of maintaining a herd of cattle and making it prosper.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eleven qualities is capable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the eleven?
Here, monks, a monk is one who knows form, he is skilled in characteristics, and he is a remover of flies.
He bandages wounds; he applies medicinal smoke; he knows the watering place; he knows when the water has been drunk;

he knows the path; he is skilled in pastures; he milks with a remainder left; and he honors with extra veneration those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, and who are the fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha.
And how, monks, is a monk one who knows form?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "Whatever form there is, all that consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who knows form.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in characteristics?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "The fool is characterized by his actions; the wise person is characterized by his actions.
In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in characteristics.
And how, monks, is a monk one who removes flies?
Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent.
[He does not tolerate] a thought of ill will that has arisen… a thought of cruelty that has arisen… whatever [unwholesome thoughts] have arisen...
He does not tolerate evil, unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who removes flies.
And how, monks, is a monk a healer of wounds?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the eye-faculty and achieves restraint over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics;
for if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
If unwholesome states were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and achieves restraint over the mind-faculty.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who covers the wound.
And how, monks, is a monk a maker of smoke?
"Here, monks, a monk teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and exactly as he has mastered it.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who produces smoke.
And how, monks, does a monk know the ford?"

In this case, monks, a monk approaches from time to time those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Matikas, and he questions them and inquires:
"Venerable sirs, what is this? What is the meaning of this?
Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been clarified, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that are grounds for uncertainty.
In this way, monks, a monk knows the ford.
And how, monks, does a monk know what has been drunk?
Here, monks, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
In this way, monks, a monk knows what has been drunk.
And how, monks, does a monk know the path?
Here, monks, a monk understands the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is.
In this way, monks, a monk knows the path.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the pasture?
Here, monks, a monk understands the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are.
In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in his range.
And how, monks, is a monk one who milks with remainder?
Here, monks, faithful householders invite a monk, bringing forth robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
In this regard, a monk knows the proper measure in receiving.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk milks the cow with something left over.

And how, monks, does a monk honor with extra veneration those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been in the Saṅgha for a long time, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha?

In this case, monks, a monk maintains bodily action imbued with loving-kindness toward those elders who have long been ordained, who have been long gone forth, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha—
both openly and in private; he maintains verbal action imbued with loving-kindness… he maintains mental action imbued with loving-kindness toward them both openly and in private.
"In this way, monks, a monk honors with superlative honor those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have long gone forth, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha.
Endowed with these eleven qualities, monks, a monk is capable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Thus was the seventh [sutta].
